scope: Measured course narration for the selected regression scenes. Each scene starts at zero and keeps its authored holds. Prior recording provenance is retained separately.

changed.previousSay: Measure proposal wait time, reviewer response time, workflow expiry, and whether reviewers catch seeded defects in non-executing exercises. Pair the approval rate with these measures to evaluate review effectiveness.

Keep action proposals, decisions, dispatch, and results as separate records. Give each one the same operation identity and proposal digest. That makes retries and investigations traceable across services.

A safe approval workflow persists exact intent, authenticates the reviewer, enforces live preconditions with the write, and verifies its receipt. The next design question is which effects need a human before execution begins.

Vega's typed proposal enters a pending state while the host validates policy. The durable record stores the action, target revision, expiry, reviewer rule, and operation identity before anyone receives a review request.
After the pending record commits, the system can notify Casey. If the worker restarts while Casey reviews, another worker can recover the pending action from durable state.

A sleeping thread or open web request stores its wait in process memory. That memory can vanish during a restart. Checkpointed workflows resume from persisted state, while replay can run code again and needs safe side-effect boundaries.

Two reviewers can race on the same pending proposal. Authenticate each, then let one guarded database update decide the winner. Match approval identity, tenant, pending status, expected version, full digest and non-expired database time. Require exactly one affected row. An earlier application expiry check can become stale before the transaction. An edit needs the same conditional guard.

The article SQLite fixture starts at synthetic time one hundred, with expiry one hundred twenty and pending version three. An exact-expiry decision is blocked. Two connections race using BEGIN IMMEDIATE: one authorizes, one is blocked, and one outbox row commits. A separate injected failure after the update but before the outbox insertion rolls back to pending with zero messages. These are executed local database results, not remote deployment or power-loss tests.

An outbox stores the decision and durable instruction to resume in the same transaction. Its dispatcher may deliver more than once. Deduplicate by decision identity and reload the protected grant; never infer executed from authorized. Rejection also needs a durable resume disposition without a write. A decision-store read or graph checkpoint in another system is advisory unless the required authoritative transition enforces its guard.
Casey opens the packet for deployment revision three. Another operator changes the deployment to revision four before the approval arrives. The old packet still names version three.
At execution, the writer compares the approved revision with live state in the same guarded mutation. A mismatch marks the old approval stale and stops the write.

Rebuild the evidence and proposal for revision four, then request the review that policy requires. A version check that runs separately from the write can still race with another update.
 Zero changed rows means some guarded predicate failed; reload authorized state to classify missing resource, stale revision or another mismatch. Advance the deployment generation on relevant changes, including rollback, so an old generation number cannot become current again. A resource revision does not cover a role or policy change in another service; enforce coordinated conditions where possible and name the remaining race.

A fresh approval reaches an execution worker. The worker claims the operation and sends the target a stable idempotency key. The target applies the traffic change, but the response disappears on the network.
A timeout leaves the execution state unknown. Query the target with the original operation identity and record its receipt. If the destination supports idempotent retries, reuse that identity.

Keep authorized, executing, executed, failed, and unknown as distinct states. An approved action may never run. A failed response may follow a successful write. Reconcile uncertain outcomes before choosing a retry.

Try a fresh case. The protected packet approves deployment revision fifty-eight and a fifteen-percent target. The live service changes to revision fifty-nine before execution. The approved digest still matches. Predict whether that matching digest permits the write.
It does not: the live precondition fails, so rebuild evidence and proposal and obtain the policy-required decision. Do not fall back to an unconditional write.

In a separate approved execution, the target accepts the conditional effect but the network reply is lost. Keep the operation unknown locally until a trusted receipt or supported same-key retry reconciles it. Do not invent a new logical identity to escape uncertainty. If the service has no suitable conditional mutation or repeat-safety contract, preserve that limitation instead of claiming a local ledger made the remote effect atomic.

Localize the broken boundary. A vanished card suggests nondurable pending state. An authorized decision without resumption suggests a missing durable dispatch path. A wrong-tenant effect suggests confused identities. An edited proposal under an old digest breaks intent. High approval with poor seeded-defect detection calls for a better review process. Each repair must retain the original operation evidence and re-establish the actual failed contract. The coding-agent workflow next turns a requested behavior into a bounded patch and executable evidence, keeping implementation, review and integration authority distinct.

beats.say: These six practice packets never reach a live writer. Start with packet one. It entered the queue at zero seconds. Casey opened it at four and decided at ten. Its queue wait is four minus zero, or four seconds. Casey’s review took ten minus four, or six seconds. Across the five opened packets, the mean wait was five point two seconds. The five decisions took six point four seconds on average after opening. Keep both times beside the approval rate.

At twenty-five seconds, five packets have decisions. Packet four expired unopened. Three decisions were approvals. An approval rate of three out of five tells us how often the reviewers said yes. Did they catch every planted defect? Compare the known condition with the decision on the same row.

They caught two out of three. Look at packet three. It carried a known defect and got approved. Count false alarms on clean reviewed packets as well. If a queue keeps passing defective packets, inspect what reviewers see and how much time they have. For live investigations, keep the proposal, decision, dispatch and trusted result linked by operation key and digest. That lets you find the boundary where evidence stops.

The promotion needs review. The host prepares a row with the scoped action, its digest and version, the required deployment revision, the evidence references, who may decide and when review expires. It adds the operation key and commits the pending record. Casey can now be notified.

Now notify Casey. While she reads, the first worker stops. Its open request is gone. Watch the key in the stored row. A replacement worker reads that same row and recovers the original action. Casey can still decide.

A sleeping thread or an unfinished web request lasts only as long as its process. If a card vanishes after a restart, check where the pending record lived. Resume from durable state and use the recorded arguments. Asking the model to reconstruct them would create a new proposal. If nobody responds before expiry, close the request without a write.

Two eligible reviewers open the same pending request. Put the status check in the database update. It must match this tenant, approval, version and full digest, and the deadline must still be open at database time. One changed row wins the decision. If someone already decided, the next update finds no pending row. Give edits the same guard.

Try the local SQLite example at clock tick one hundred. The packet expires at one hundred twenty. A click at that exact deadline is blocked. Now race two connections before expiry. Each requests a write transaction with begin immediate. One authorizes, one is blocked, and one outbox row commits. In a separate run, stop after the update and before inserting the message. The transaction rolls back to pending with zero messages.

The table holding that message is the outbox. If the worker stops after commit, the resume instruction is already there with the decision. A dispatcher can deliver the same message twice. Deduplicate by decision identity and reload the protected grant. A rejection also resumes the workflow, so it can end without a write. If a recorded approval never resumes, follow its outbox entry. The deployment receipt belongs to a later step.

Back at the router, run Casey’s original twenty-five percent packet on two copies of the same deployment. Both start in shadow at revision three. The worker has a current grant for this service. Read the last line of its update. The database checks the revision as part of the write. Leave the left deployment alone. On the right, another operator puts ten percent of traffic on the canary. That advances its revision to four. Casey’s stored packet and digest stay fixed. When the same statement returns on each side, what percentage will each canary serve?

On the left, one row changes. The canary serves twenty-five percent. On the right, zero rows change. Ten percent stays live. Zero rows tells us that a condition failed. Reload the row to find out why. Here it exists, and its revision changed. A mismatch marks the old approval stale and stops the write. Both deployments now say revision four. Only the left one got there through Casey’s write.

Build a new packet for revision four. Attach the new run and evaluation, then request a fresh review. This proposal would move the right-hand canary from ten to twenty-five percent. The worker needs a new decision before it can write.

Retain the old decision in the history. Advance the revision on every relevant change, even a rollback. Checking it before the write would leave time for a competing update. Check roles and policy separately when another service owns them.

Follow the right-hand deployment. Casey has now approved the new packet for revision four. The worker claims the operation and sends the target a stable idempotency key. The request asks for twenty-five percent. The target applies the traffic change. It saves a receipt under that key, but the response disappears on the network. Now stand at the worker. Its timer expires. What outcome can it record from the timeout alone?

A timeout leaves the execution state unknown. Query the target with the original operation identity. The reply names this operation, the twenty-five percent share and revision five. The worker can now record its receipt.
Look at the router. It moved traffic from ten to twenty-five percent once. Reading the receipt moves no traffic. The change at the worker is what it can now prove.

A definite failure and a missing reply need different handling. If the result is still unknown, inspect it before another attempt. A repeat is safe only for identical parameters under a key the destination still honors. If that contract is missing or the key has expired, keep the outcome open for reconciliation. A fresh key could apply a second effect.

Try a fresh release. These are two possible histories of the same router. Each starts at five percent, at revision fifty-eight. Casey approves fifteen percent for that revision. Both workers have the right packet, the current grant and the same logical operation key. On the left, another operator gets there first and sets fifteen percent. The revision advances to fifty-nine. The approved digest still matches. Predict whether that matching digest permits the write.

It does not: the left router requires a match on the deployment revision. Vega’s guarded update returns zero rows. Reloading the row explains why the precondition failed. Close that stale attempt. Now follow the right-hand worker. It sends the same approved update while the revision still matches.

On the way back, the network reply is lost. The right-hand worker times out. A later read shows fifteen percent at revision fifty-nine on both routers. Which worker still needs a receipt lookup to find out whether its write happened?

The worker on the right. Someone else could have produced exactly that traffic reading, as the left-hand router shows. Look up the key Vega sent on the right. The destination returns the receipt for that operation, recording fifteen percent at revision fifty-nine. Now the worker can mark it executed. Both traffic strips stay still. What changed was our evidence of who moved the traffic.
